title: The Water Climbed 481 Metres: Alaska's Megatsunami Explained
description:
On 10 August 2025, more than 64 million cubic metres of rock fell into Tracy Arm fjord in Alaska, and the water ran 481 metres (1,578 ft) up the fjord wall. That's the second-highest tsunami run-up ever recorded. But the wave itself wasn't 481 metres tall. Here's how that works.

In this first episode of Hopeverse Media, the Navigator, Rio and Lumen unpack the Tracy Arm landslide tsunami, using findings published in Science on 6 May 2026 (Shugar et al.).

🔭 What you'll learn
• Run-up vs wave height: simulations put the wave at about 100 m (330 ft), yet momentum carried water 481 m up the fjord wall at simulated impact speeds over 150 mph (≈250 km/h)
• Trimlines: how stripped trees record how high the water reached
• Landslide vs earthquake tsunamis: tall and local vs long, low and ocean-crossing
• How Tracy Arm compares with the record, Lituya Bay (1958, about 524 m)
• Why glacier retreat driven by climate change "preconditioned" the slope, and why the exact trigger is still uncertain (rain is only a possible factor)
• The magnitude-5.4-equivalent seismic signal, and the days-long seiche detected worldwide, only the second known after Dickson Fjord, Greenland (2023)
• The seismic "hum" that sped up before the collapse but was only found afterwards, and the co-authors' argument that monitoring could have allowed a yellow alert about a day ahead and an orange alert in the final hours. No such US program currently exists.
• Who was there: no injuries were reported. Kayakers lost gear, and one cruise ship had left about 12 hours earlier.

=== FINAL SCRIPT (fact-checked by Mr. Focus) ===
[0:00] RIO: "Wait— the water climbed 481 metres up a cliff?"
[0:03] NAV: "Let's find out. On 10 August 2025, at 5:26 in the morning, a mountainside in Southeast Alaska gave way. What followed was the second-highest tsunami run-up ever recorded. There's no known footage of the wave itself, so everything you'll see is an illustration, rebuilt from evidence the water left behind." [TITLE CARD 0:27–0:29]
S1 [0:29] NAV: "This is Tracy Arm, a narrow fjord south-east of Juneau, near South Sawyer Glacier. A study published in Science in May 2026, led by Dan Shugar of the University of Calgary with 18 co-authors, including seismologists at the Alaska Earthquake Center, reconstructed what happened. More than 64 million cubic metres of rock, about 2.3 billion cubic feet, and that's a minimum, dropped roughly a kilometre onto the glacier and into the fjord. The water surged across the fjord… and kept going up." RIO: "Hold on… was anyone there?" NAV: "Kayakers camped on Harbor Island lost their gear, and a small cruise ship in nearby Endicott Arm felt strong currents. But no one was injured."
S2 [1:24] RIO: "Wait— so the wave itself was that tall?" NAV: "That's the most common mix-up. Wave height is how tall the wave stands on the water. Run-up is the highest elevation the water reaches on land. 481 metres, 1,578 feet. That's how high the water climbed. The wave itself? Computer simulations put it at about 100 metres, around 330 feet, when it hit the far shore. Enormous, but roughly a fifth of the run-up." RIO: "Okay, the wave is one number and the climb is another."
S3 [2:04] RIO: "But how does a 100-metre wave climb almost five times higher?" NAV: "Momentum. When fast water slams into a steep wall, its speed carries it upward, like a skateboarder up a ramp. Back-of-envelope: ignoring friction, rising 481 metres takes about 97 metres per second, roughly 350 km/h. Real simulations put the impact speed lower, over 150 miles per hour, about 70 metres per second, because the wave was already about 100 metres tall when it hit."
S4 [2:44] RIO: "If nobody filmed it, how do we know how high it went?" NAV: "The mountainside kept a record. Where the water reached, it stripped away trees and soil, leaving a sharp line called a trimline. Measure it, and you have the run-up; a field survey later confirmed it."
S5 [3:08] NAV: "The record holder is also in Alaska: Lituya Bay, 1958, about 524 metres, 1,720 feet, also from trimlines. There, an earthquake triggered a rockslide, and the rockslide made the wave." RIO: "Wait— so why don't these cross oceans like the big earthquake tsunamis?" NAV: "In a big earthquake tsunami, the seafloor shifts a few metres over hundreds of kilometres, lifting a long, low wave with huge energy that can cross oceans. A landslide dumps a big mass into one spot. Squeezed into a narrow fjord, the wave gets very tall locally, but it spreads from a point, breaks into shorter waves and carries far less energy, so it fades fast." RIO: "Earthquake waves are low and travel far. Landslide waves are tall and stay local." NAV: "Exactly."
S6 [4:03] RIO: "Mountains don't just fall over. What changed?" NAV: "Ice. South Sawyer Glacier used to brace the base of that slope, like a buttress on a cathedral. It had retreated several hundred metres, more than a third of a mile in just the previous two months, with a burst of rapid retreat from 2 to 5 August. The paper says this glacial retreat, caused by climate change, preconditioned the slope: it set the stage." RIO: "So what made it go that morning?" NAV: "That's still uncertain. Rain had fallen, though sources disagree on how heavy, so it's a possible factor, not a confirmed cause. And it's not unique: in 2015, Alaska's Taan Fiord had a run-up of about 193 metres, also linked to glacier retreat."
S7 [5:03] NAV: "The collapse sent out a seismic signal equivalent to a magnitude 5.4 earthquake. Then the water in Tracy Arm kept sloshing for more than a day. That's called a seiche, and seismometers around the world picked it up. It's only the second days-long seiche ever detected worldwide like this; the first was Dickson Fjord, Greenland, in 2023."
S8 [5:36, kept whole] NAV: "So was there any warning? Let's ask someone who listens to the ground." LISTENER: "Looking back, yes. For several days, the slope gave off tiny seismic signals, around magnitude 1 to 2, about an hour apart. In the last six hours they came every 30 to 60 seconds, and about two hours before the collapse they merged into one continuous hum, called tremor. But here's the catch: nobody saw this at the time. The signals were only found afterwards, because that area wasn't covered by automatic landslide detection." NAV: "Could an alert have worked?" LISTENER: "Two of the study's co-authors argue, in an opinion piece, that with monitoring, a yellow alert could have been justified about a day ahead, based on the weather and rapid glacier retreat, and an orange alert in the final hours as the signals surged. No program like that exists in the US today, and warning science is still young. A signal worth watching, not a prediction."
S9 [7:00] NAV: "Why does this matter? On busy summer days, up to six cruise ships visit this fjord. One, the Hanse Explorer, left the glacier the evening before, about twelve hours earlier. No one was hurt, and several cruise lines changed their 2026 itineraries to avoid the area."
S10 [7:20] NAV: "What exactly tipped the slope over? If alerts become possible, who would run them? And which other fjords might already be primed? Those questions are still open."
OUTRO [7:34–7:55] NAV: "Here's the hopeful part: the mountain whispered before it fell. Nobody heard it in time, but we're learning how to listen. If this sparked a question, drop it below, and subscribe for the next one. Stay curious. See you in the next corner of the Hopeverse."
